timeline.place: Miyamoto, Harima or Mimasaka Province, Japan
timeline.title: Born in a village called Miyamoto
timeline.text: Musashi was born around 1584, though some sources say 1583. In The Book of Five Rings he says he was born in Harima Province, but one historian places his home village in Mimasaka Province. His father was Shinmen Munisai, a swordsman and master of the jutte, a short iron truncheon.

timeline.title: First duel, against Arima Kihei
timeline.text: As a boy he fought and beat Arima Kihei, a trained swordsman of the Kashima Shinto school. One account dates this to 1596. Accounts give his age as anywhere from about 11 to 13.

timeline.title: Second duel, at about sixteen
timeline.text: He defeated Tadashima Akiyama, a swordsman from Tajima Province. Sources disagree on whether he was 15 or 16 at the time.

timeline.title: The year of Sekigahara
timeline.text: This was the year of the great battle of Sekigahara. Older accounts put Musashi on the losing Western side, but later research suggests he fought for the Eastern side under Kuroda Yoshitaka, at Ishigakihara and Fuka Castle in Kyushu. Whether he was at Sekigahara itself is still debated.

timeline.title: Challenging the Yoshioka school
timeline.text: In Kyoto he challenged the Yoshioka, a famous family school of swordsmanship. He first beat its head, Yoshioka Seijuro, on Rendai Moor.

timeline.title: Denshichiro and the pine at Ichijo-ji
timeline.text: He then defeated Seijuro's brother Denshichiro. A third match against the young Matashichiro was fought by a pine tree at Ichijo-ji, and ended the Yoshioka challenge.

timeline.title: Years on the road
timeline.text: He spent the following years travelling and testing himself against other fighters. Recorded opponents include Okuzoin Doei of the Hozoin spear school in Nara and a sickle-and-chain fighter named Shishido. Exact dates for many of these meetings are not known.

timeline.title: Meeting Muso Gonnosuke
timeline.text: In Edo, the city that is now Tokyo, he faced Muso Gonnosuke, a master of the staff. Other duels in Edo, against Hayashi Osedo and Tsujikaze Tenma, are dated to 1610.

timeline.title: The duel on Ganryu Island
timeline.text: He fought Sasaki Kojiro on a small island off Shimonoseki, and Kojiro was killed. Tradition says Musashi arrived late and carved a wooden sword from a boat oar on the way, but there are differing accounts of how the duel really went. The island, once called Funa-jima, was later named after Kojiro's Ganryu school.

timeline.title: The sieges of Osaka
timeline.text: He is believed to have served under the lord Mizuno Katsushige during the Osaka campaigns of 1614 and 1615, carrying a banner and guarding the lord's son. No important deeds of his there are documented.

timeline.title: Duel with Miyake Gunbei
timeline.text: In Tatsuno he defeated Miyake Gunbei. By this time his reputation as a fighter was well established.

timeline.title: Adopting Iori
timeline.text: While living in Edo he adopted a boy of about eleven, who became Miyamoto Iori. Iori later served the Ogasawara clan and rose to become one of its leading retainers.

timeline.title: Loss of his son Mikinosuke
timeline.text: His earlier adopted son Mikinosuke, who had served in the Osaka campaign, took his own life in 1626. He followed the samurai custom of junshi, dying after the death of one's lord.

timeline.title: Meeting in Owari
timeline.text: In Nagoya he met Yagyu Hyogonosuke, a leading swordsman of the Yagyu school. In 1641 one of his followers, Hirao Yoemon, became master of arms for the Owari domain.

timeline.title: Guest of the Ogasawara
timeline.text: He moved to Kokura with Iori as a guest of the lord Ogasawara Tadazane. That same year he is recorded as defeating Takada Matabei, a spear specialist.

timeline.title: The Shimabara Rebellion
timeline.text: He took part in putting down the Shimabara Rebellion, the only battle service of his that is clearly documented. One record says he was knocked from his horse by a stone thrown by a peasant. Iori's stipend was raised that year for his part in the siege.

timeline.title: Retainer of the Hosokawa clan
timeline.text: He became an official retainer of Hosokawa Tadatoshi, lord of Kumamoto, with a stipend of 300 koku and a residence on the grounds of Chiba Castle. He had been connected with Tadatoshi for some years before, though accounts differ on the dates. Around this time he chose students to carry on his school.

timeline.title: Thirty-five Instructions on Strategy
timeline.text: He wrote the Hyoho Sanju Go, thirty-five instructions on strategy, for Lord Tadatoshi. It became the basis of The Book of Five Rings.

timeline.title: Failing health
timeline.text: He began to suffer attacks of neuralgia, a nerve pain. His health would not recover.

timeline.title: Retreat to the Reigando cave
timeline.text: He withdrew to Reigando, the Spirit Rock Cave west of Kumamoto, to live simply and write. He spent many of his final months there.

timeline.title: The Book of Five Rings is finished
timeline.text: In the second month of 1645 he finished The Book of Five Rings, written in five books named Earth, Water, Fire, Wind and Void. It set down the teachings of his school for his students.

timeline.title: The Dokkodo and a final gift
timeline.text: About a week before his death he wrote the Dokkodo, 21 short precepts on living alone with discipline. He gave it, with the manuscript of The Book of Five Rings, to his closest student, Terao Magonojo.

timeline.title: Death
timeline.text: Musashi died on 13 June 1645, aged about 60 to 62, possibly of lung cancer. One record says he died in the Reigando cave, another at his house in Kumamoto. A tomb was set up for him on Mount Iwato on his lord's orders.

works.title: The Book of Five Rings (Go Rin no Sho)
works.text: His book on strategy and swordsmanship, written between 1643 and 1645 to record what he taught his students. It is divided into five books.

works.title: The Earth Book
works.text: An introduction to strategy that compares learning a craft to building a house. It ends with nine practical principles for students.

works.title: The Water Book
works.text: Describes his own style: basic technique, a calm and balanced spirit, stance, and the five attitudes of holding the sword.

works.title: The Fire Book
works.text: About the heat of a fight: reading the situation, acting first, and timing in both single combat and group battle.

works.title: The Wind Book
works.text: A critique of rival schools of swordsmanship. The Japanese word for wind can also mean style.

works.title: The Book of the Void
works.text: A short closing book on knowledge, the mind and emptiness, shaped by Zen Buddhism.

works.title: Hyoho Sanju Go (Thirty-five Instructions on Strategy)
works.text: Written for Lord Hosokawa Tadatoshi. It laid the groundwork for The Book of Five Rings.

works.title: Dokkodo (The Path of Aloneness)
works.text: Twenty-one short precepts written about a week before he died, for his student Terao Magonojo. It reads as a condensed version of his earlier teaching.

works.title: Hyoho Niten Ichi-ryu
works.text: His school of fighting with the long and short sword together, founded some time between 1604 and 1640. It is still taught today, and Japan's classical martial arts associations recognise its main line as heir to his tradition.

works.title: Shrike in a Barren Tree (Koboku Meigeki-zu)
works.text: An ink painting on paper of a shrike perched on a dead branch, his best-known picture. It is held by the Kuboso Memorial Museum of Arts in Izumi and listed as an Important Cultural Property. The exact year is unknown.

works.title: Wild Geese and Reeds (Rogan-zu)
works.text: A pair of six-panel folding screens in ink, attributed to Musashi and held by the Eisei Bunko Museum in Tokyo, home of the Hosokawa family collection. The exact year is unknown.

works.title: Hotei Watching a Cockfight
works.text: An ink painting of the cheerful monk Hotei watching two roosters fight, dated about 1630 to 1645 in image records. The sources we opened do not say which museum holds it.

works.title: Red Plum and Doves
works.text: A hanging scroll in ink on paper, made in the Edo period. It was named an Important Cultural Property in 1959 and is held by the Eisei Bunko Museum.

works.title: Calligraphy and ink painting
works.text: Besides fighting and writing, he practised calligraphy and ink painting, especially the broken ink style. The Book of Five Rings urges students to train in other arts too.

works.title: Wooden sword (Jisso Enman no Bokuto)
works.text: A long red oak wooden sword that his school says he made, kept at Usa Jingu shrine in Oita and not on public display. Its shape suggests he used it as a staff in his later years.

books.title: A Book of Five Rings
books.author: Miyamoto Musashi, translated by Victor Harris
books.note: The first English translation, published by Overlook Press. We did not find a verified public domain English translation online, so we link none.

books.title: Dokkodo
books.author: Miyamoto Musashi, translated by Colin Hyakutake-Watkin
books.note: His 21 last precepts. The translation dates from 1992 and can be read on hyoho.com, but it is copyrighted, not public domain.

books.title: The Complete Musashi: The Book of Five Rings and Other Works
books.author: Miyamoto Musashi, translated by Alex Bennett
books.note: A modern translation (Tuttle) that also includes his shorter writings, among them Combat Strategy in 35 Articles and The Path Walked Alone. An earlier edition appeared in 2018.

books.title: The Lone Samurai: The Life of Miyamoto Musashi
books.author: William Scott Wilson
books.note: A biography by a translator of The Book of Five Rings, covering his travels, duels, teaching, art and writing. Reviewers note how few primary sources survive.
